WHO classifies astrocytomas into four prognostic grades based on histologic features: 
grade I (pilocytic astrocytoma, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma) 
grade II (diffuse astrocytoma) 
grade III (anaplastic astrocytoma) 
grade IV (glioblastoma).
Glioblastoma accounts for the majority of high-grade astrocytomas.

qs.q: Glioblastoma can stimulate its own growth by producing platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and simultaneously expressing its receptor. This phenomenon is best described as:
qs.e: Autocrine stimulation occurs when the tumor cell makes the growth factor and also expresses its receptor, thereby stimulating itself. This is distinct from paracrine signaling where signals act on neighboring cells.

qs.q: Glioblastoma cells often secrete platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) while simultaneously expressing its corresponding receptor on their surface. This form of self-stimulation is known as:
qs.e: Autocrine stimulation occurs when a tumor cell produces a growth factor and also expresses its receptor, continuously stimulating its own growth. Paracrine signaling involves factors acting on neighboring cells instead.

qs.q: Hepatocyte growth factor/scatter factor (HGF/SCF) is found at high concentrations at the advancing edges of glioblastoma multiforme. What is its primary role?
o: Inducing apoptosis in leading edge cells
qs.e: ** HGF/SCF is a paracrine effector of cell motility produced by stromal cells. Its elevated concentration at the advancing edges of highly invasive tumors like glioblastoma supports its role in promoting tumor cell locomotion and invasion.
